patient.name: Kwame Boateng
patient.complaint: Severe perineal and scrotal pain with fever for 36 hours
background: Type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin (an SGLT-2 inhibitor)
Small perianal boil a week ago, squeezed it himself

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a red, swollen limb or perineum where the pain is far worse than the skin looks and the patient is septic: the answer is necrotising fasciitis, not cellulitis.

points: Squeezed a perianal boil a week ago.
Now **agonising** perineal and scrotal pain for 36 hours.

steps.lead: A minor skin breach (the boil) followed by a fast, deep, painful infection: this is the story of **necrotising fasciitis**.
Kwame has the major risk factor, **diabetes**, and takes an **SGLT-2 inhibitor**, which is specifically linked to perineal disease.

points: Scrotum and perineum: dusky red, swollen, **poorly demarcated** edge.
He screams when you barely touch the skin.
A small **black patch** on the left scrotum.
Fine **crackling** under the fingers at the edge.

steps.lead: Kwame's pain is far worse than the redness suggests, and the black patch and crepitus are **late signs** of necrosis and gas.

steps.q: Which single feature most separates Kwame's illness from simple cellulitis?
o: Pain out of proportion to the skin findings
steps.r: Fever, redness and a raised CRP all occur in cellulitis. **Pain out of proportion** to examination plus systemic illness is the hallmark of necrotising fasciitis.

steps.lead: Disproportionate pain, sepsis and a poorly defined, darkening edge: Kwame is not a cellulitis to send home with oral antibiotics.

steps.title: Cellulitis vs necrotising fasciitis vs gas gangrene
head: Feature
Cellulitis
Necrotising fasciitis
Gas gangrene

steps.lead: Kwame's disease is in the scrotum and perineum: this is **Fournier's gangrene**, in the most commonly affected site overall.
Kwame is already hypotensive: without urgent surgery the next steps are **septic shock**, organ failure and death.

steps.text: Do not be reassured by **mild-looking skin**. The infection spreads under the skin first, so the surface lags behind. Severe pain plus sepsis means necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise.

investigation.exam: Expect a question where the right answer is that this is a **clinical diagnosis** and imaging must not delay theatre, or one asking what the bloods or ultrasound will show.

steps.q: The registrar suspects necrotising fasciitis. What confirms it?
steps.r: It is **primarily a clinical diagnosis**. Tests support it, but the decision to operate is clinical; findings at surgery confirm it.

steps.lead: Kwame's diagnosis is made at the bedside. A quick **bedside ultrasound** showing fluid and air along the fascia supports a deep infection.

steps.title: Kwame's bloods and venous gas
steps.text: Very high CRP and WCC with a **metabolic (lactic) acidosis** and an AKI: a septic, deep infection.

steps.lead: Kwame's **CRP, WCC and acidosis** fit. A CT would show gas, but he is shocked: **imaging must never delay surgery**.

visual.title: Lactate
visual.label: Kwame 4.6
visual.caption: A lactate above 4 means poor tissue perfusion: Kwame needs fluids, antibiotics and theatre now.

steps.title: Tests run alongside, never instead of, surgery
nodes: Clinical suspicion: pain out of proportion + sepsis
Bedside ultrasound if it is quick
CT/MRI only if it will not delay theatre
steps.caption: A normal scan does not exclude necrotising fasciitis.

steps.text: The tempting answer is **'CT/MRI to confirm'**. In a septic patient with suspected necrotising fasciitis the next step is the surgeon and theatre, not the scanner.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate definitive / next step in management?': the answer is **emergency surgical debridement**, with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and the Sepsis Six alongside.

points: BP 88/52 mmHg after 500 mL of fluid.
Urology and general surgery called to the bedside.

steps.q: What is the definitive treatment for Kwame?
o: IV antibiotics and review in 24 hours
steps.r: **Emergency surgical debridement** of all dead tissue is definitive. Antibiotics alone cannot reach dead, thrombosed tissue.

steps.lead: Kwame goes to theatre tonight: the surgeons cut away all **necrotic tissue** and usually return within 24 to 48 hours to look again.

steps.title: Kwame's first hour (Sepsis Six) while theatre is prepared
steps.caption: Resuscitation and antibiotics happen at the same time as calling the surgeons.

steps.lead: Kwame gets **piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin**, fluids and the **Sepsis Six**, then critical care after surgery.

steps.text: **Clindamycin** is added because it switches off bacterial **toxin production** (it is a protein synthesis inhibitor), which matters in Group A Strep disease.

visual.title: Kwame after debridement
visual.caption: Lactate falls quickly once dead tissue is removed; CRP lags behind by days.

steps.lead: Kwame's resuscitation follows the **Sepsis Six** and Surviving Sepsis guidance: antibiotics within the hour, fluids, lactate and source control.

steps.text: **Oral antibiotics, elevation and review** is the cellulitis answer. For necrotising fasciitis it is a fatal delay.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the usual organism (Group A Strep), the organism of gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens), why the skin turns black, or why SGLT-2 inhibitors are linked to Fournier's gangrene.

steps.lead: Kwame's perineal infection is probably **polymicrobial (type 1)**; a limb infection after a cut in a young person is more often **Group A Strep (type 2)**.

steps.title: From boil to septic shock
nodes: Bacteria enter through a skin breach
Toxins and enzymes spread along fascial planes

steps.lead: Kwame's **black patch** is skin that has lost its blood supply after the small vessels feeding it **thrombosed**.
Each hour Kwame waited for surgery the infection spread further along the fascia and more **toxin** entered his blood.

steps.q: Why does empagliflozin raise Kwame's risk of Fournier's gangrene?
o: It causes glycosuria that feeds genital bacteria
steps.r: SGLT-2 inhibitors block glucose reabsorption in the kidney, so urine is full of **glucose**, which promotes bacterial growth in the genital region.

steps.lead: Kwame's sugary urine around the perineum gave the bacteria a growth medium; his **empagliflozin** should be stopped.
Kwame's crepitus is gas from bacteria. In **gas gangrene**, Clostridium perfringens **alpha-toxin** destroys muscle and produces much more gas.

visual.title: Hours from arrival to debridement
visual.label: Kwame 4 h
visual.caption: Delay to debridement is the strongest modifiable factor for death.

steps.text: Exam pairs: **Group A Strep** = type 2, limb, healthy person. **Polymicrobial** = type 1, perineum, diabetic. **Clostridium perfringens** = gas gangrene, crepitus, myonecrosis.

mcq.q: What is the hallmark feature of necrotising fasciitis?
o: Pain out of proportion to examination
mcq.r: **Pain out of proportion** to examination findings is the hallmark.

o: Necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum or vulva
mcq.r: Fournier's gangrene is **necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum/vulva**.

mcq.q: What is the most commonly affected site overall?
mcq.r: The notes give the **perineum** as the most common site overall.

mcq.q: Which drug class is a risk factor in diabetic patients?
mcq.r: **SGLT-2 inhibitors** (the gliflozins) are linked to Fournier's gangrene.
It is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**; imaging must never delay surgery.

mcq.q: What does ultrasound show in deep soft-tissue infection?
o: Fluid and air between fascial layers
mcq.r: **Fluid and air between fascial layers** indicates a deeper infection.

mcq.q: Which empirical IV antibiotic regimen is used?
mcq.r: **Pip-taz plus clindamycin**, or meropenem plus clindamycin.

mcq.q: What is the most common organism in type 2 necrotising fasciitis?
mcq.r: Type 2 is most commonly **Group A Streptococcus** (Streptococcus pyogenes).
**Clostridium perfringens** alpha-toxin causes myonecrosis and gas.

prompts.q: What is necrotising fasciitis and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem hides a risk factor, often diabetes or IV drug use.

points.p: Rapidly progressive infection of deep fascia and subcutaneous tissue causing necrosis
points.why: 'Flesh-eating disease'; it spreads along the fascial planes.

points.p: Usually follows minor injury or surgery
points.why: Often a trivial breach in the skin.

points.p: Diabetes is the major risk factor (SGLT-2 inhibitors)
points.why: SGLT-2 inhibitors are specifically linked to Fournier's.

points.p: Immunosuppression, recent surgery, IV drug use
points.why: An injecting drug user with a painful thigh is a classic stem.

prompts.q: How does necrotising fasciitis present, early and late?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the early signs are subtle; the pain is not.

points.p: Pain out of proportion to examination findings
points.why: The single most important clue.

points.p: Rapidly spreading erythema, swelling, tenderness
points.why: Mark the edge: spread over hours is a red flag.

points.p: Fever and systemic illness
points.why: Tachycardia and hypotension point to deep infection.

points.p: Late: blistering, bullae, crepitus, black necrotic skin
points.why: By the time these appear, the infection is advanced.

prompts.q: Which features tell you it is necrotising fasciitis rather than cellulitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: both are red, hot and swollen; look for what cellulitis does not do.

points.p: Pain disproportionate to the exam findings
points.why: Cellulitis pain matches the redness.

points.p: Accompanying systemic illness
points.why: Cellulitis patients are usually not shocked.

points.p: Poorly demarcated erythema, may look gangrenous later
points.why: Sharply demarcated, raised erythema suggests erysipelas instead.

prompts.q: What are gas gangrene and Fournier's gangrene, and what is the commonest site?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: crepitus after a crush injury vs a red, painful scrotum.

points.p: Gas gangrene: crepitus, caused by Clostridium perfringens
points.why: Myonecrosis with prominent gas.

points.p: Fournier's gangrene: necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum or vulva
points.why: Think diabetes and SGLT-2 inhibitors.

points.p: Perineum is the most commonly affected site overall
points.why: Do not assume a limb.

prompts.q: What are the complications of necrotising fasciitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: this is why the answer is always urgent surgery.

points.p: Septic shock
points.why: Toxins absorbed into the blood.

points.p: Multi-organ failure
points.why: AKI, ARDS and DIC can follow.

points.p: Amputation
points.why: Extensive debridement can mean losing a limb.

points.p: Death
points.why: Mortality rises with every hour of delay.

prompts.q: How is necrotising fasciitis diagnosed, and what do the tests show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tests support, they never delay surgery.

points.p: Primarily a clinical diagnosis
points.why: Confirmed at surgery.

points.p: Ultrasound: fluid and air between fascial layers
points.why: Indicates deeper soft-tissue infection.

points.p: Bloods: raised CRP and WCC, metabolic acidosis
points.why: A raised lactate shows hypoperfusion.

points.p: CT/MRI may show gas but must never delay surgery
points.why: The classic wrong answer is 'MRI to confirm'.

prompts.q: What is the definitive management, and what goes alongside it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: surgery is the answer; antibiotics alone never are.

points.p: Emergency surgical debridement
points.why: Antibiotics cannot penetrate dead, thrombosed tissue.

points.p: IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin (or meropenem plus clindamycin)
points.why: Clindamycin reduces toxin production.

points.p: IV fluids and the Sepsis Six
points.why: Antibiotics within the hour.

points.p: Critical care support
points.why: Most need ITU after surgery.

prompts.q: What are the six parts of the Sepsis Six?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three in, three out.

points.p: Give oxygen
points.why: To target saturations.

points.p: Take blood cultures
points.why: Before antibiotics, but do not delay them.

points.p: Give IV antibiotics
points.why: Within one hour.

points.p: Give IV fluids
points.why: Crystalloid bolus if hypotensive or lactate raised.

points.p: Measure lactate
points.why: Above 4 mmol/L is severe.

points.p: Monitor urine output
points.why: Catheterise and record hourly.

prompts.q: Which organisms cause necrotising fasciitis and gas gangrene, and how do they damage tissue?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: type 1 vs type 2, and alpha-toxin.

points.p: Type 2: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes)
points.why: Most common organism in the notes.

points.p: Type 1: polymicrobial
points.why: Typical in diabetics and the perineum.

points.p: Exotoxins and enzymes (hyaluronidase, streptokinase) destroy fascia along fascial planes
points.why: Skin and muscle are relatively spared early, so the signs lag.

points.p: Clostridium perfringens alpha-toxin causes myonecrosis and gas
points.why: This is why gas gangrene crackles.

prompts.q: Why does the skin turn black, and why are SGLT-2 inhibitors a risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the sign from the mechanism.

points.p: Thrombosis of small skin vessels causes ischaemia and necrosis
points.why: Black skin is dead skin.

points.p: SGLT-2 inhibitors cause glycosuria, promoting genital bacterial growth
points.why: Hence the link with Fournier's.

points.p: Rapid spread plus systemic toxin absorption causes quick septic shock
points.why: Delay to debridement speeds this.

glossary.Necrotising fasciitis: A rapidly spreading infection of the deep fascia and fat under the skin that kills tissue.
glossary.fascia: Sheets of connective tissue that wrap muscles; infection spreads quickly along them.
glossary.debridement: Surgical removal of dead or infected tissue.
glossary.Fournier's gangrene: Necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum, perineum or vulva.
glossary.gas gangrene: Clostridial infection of muscle that produces gas and kills muscle tissue.
glossary.crepitus: A crackling feeling under the fingers caused by gas in the tissues.
glossary.bullae: Large fluid-filled blisters on the skin.
glossary.erythema: Redness of the skin from increased blood flow.
glossary.necrosis: Death of tissue, here from infection and loss of blood supply.
glossary.cellulitis: Infection of the dermis and subcutaneous fat; pain matches the redness and patients are rarely shocked.
glossary.erysipelas: A superficial skin infection with a sharply demarcated, raised red edge.
glossary.Group A Streptococcus: Streptococcus pyogenes; the commonest cause of type 2 necrotising fasciitis.
glossary.Streptococcus pyogenes: Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus; makes toxins and spreading enzymes.
glossary.Clostridium perfringens: Anaerobic gas-forming bacterium that causes gas gangrene via alpha-toxin.
glossary.alpha-toxin: The Clostridium perfringens toxin that destroys cell membranes and muscle.
glossary.polymicrobial: Caused by several different bacteria at once (type 1 necrotising fasciitis).
glossary.hyaluronidase: A bacterial enzyme that breaks down connective tissue so infection spreads.
glossary.streptokinase: A streptococcal enzyme that breaks down clots, helping bacteria spread.
glossary.exotoxins: Toxins released by bacteria that damage tissue and cause shock.
glossary.SGLT-2 inhibitors: Diabetes drugs (gliflozins) that make the kidney pass glucose in urine.
glossary.empagliflozin: An SGLT-2 inhibitor used in type 2 diabetes and heart failure.
glossary.Sepsis Six: Oxygen, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate and urine output, all within one hour.
glossary.septic shock: Sepsis with low blood pressure needing vasopressors and a lactate above 2 despite fluids.
glossary.lactate: A marker of poor tissue perfusion; above 4 mmol/L indicates severe sepsis.
glossary.metabolic acidosis: Low blood pH from excess acid such as lactate, with a low bicarbonate.
glossary.piperacillin-tazobactam: A broad-spectrum IV penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (Tazocin).
glossary.clindamycin: A protein synthesis inhibitor antibiotic that also switches off bacterial toxin production.
glossary.meropenem: A very broad-spectrum carbapenem IV antibiotic.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation that rises in infection.
glossary.WCC: White cell count; raised in bacterial infection.
glossary.multi-organ failure: Failure of two or more organ systems, such as kidneys, lungs and clotting.
glossary.IV drug use: Injecting drugs into veins; a risk factor for deep soft-tissue infection.

technique.stem: A 47 year old man has a 2 day history of increasing pain in his right lower leg after grazing his shin while gardening. He says the pain is unbearable. There is mild, poorly demarcated erythema over the shin and he winces at light touch well beyond the red area. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a red, painful leg: decide how deep and how dangerous it is.
Minor injury, **pain out of proportion** to mild skin signs, and hypotension with tachycardia: a septic, deep infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pain far worse than the skin plus sepsis: **necrotising fasciitis**.

elim: Gout affects a joint, usually the big toe, without shock.
Cellulitis pain matches the redness and patients are rarely hypotensive.
DVT causes calf swelling, not fever and shock after a graze.
Erysipelas has a sharply demarcated, raised edge; this edge is poorly demarcated.

steps.x: **E. Necrotising fasciitis.** Rule: pain out of proportion plus systemic illness is never just cellulitis.

technique.stem: A 39 year old woman who injects heroin has severe pain in her left thigh around an injection site for 24 hours. There is a small area of dusky erythema but she cannot bear it being touched. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg. The surgical registrar suspects necrotising fasciitis and the radiology department offers an MRI in 3 hours.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to confirming the diagnosis?
o: Clinical diagnosis with immediate surgical exploration
CT of the thigh before surgical review
MRI of the thigh and await the report

steps.x: It asks how to confirm the diagnosis in a shocked patient: think about what must not be delayed.
IV drug use risk factor, pain out of proportion, shock, and a scan that would delay surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Necrotising fasciitis is a **clinical diagnosis**; she goes to theatre, where it is confirmed.

elim: CT may show gas but imaging must never delay surgery.
Waiting 3 hours for MRI in a shocked patient is a fatal delay.
Waiting 24 hours lets the infection spread along fascial planes.
A skin biopsy samples the wrong layer and delays treatment.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis with immediate surgical exploration.** Rule: imaging never delays surgery.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a 1 day history of severe scrotal pain and swelling. The scrotum is red and swollen with a black patch and crepitus. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. IV fluids, blood cultures and IV antibiotics have been started.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: IV antibiotics and repeat imaging at 24 hours

steps.x: Definitive management: the one treatment that removes the source.
Diabetic, scrotal necrosis with gas, septic: **Fournier's gangrene**. Antibiotics are already running.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dead tissue must be cut out: **emergency surgical debridement**.

elim: Oral antibiotics and elevation treat cellulitis, not necrotising fasciitis.
Hyperbaric oxygen is not definitive and must not replace surgery.
Antibiotics cannot reach thrombosed tissue; waiting 24 hours is fatal.
A catheter helps monitoring but does not treat the source.

steps.x: **B. Emergency surgical debridement.** Rule: necrotising fasciitis = theatre now, antibiotics alongside.

technique.stem: A 58 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is treated for necrotising fasciitis of the left leg. Before theatre the surgeon notes a 3 cm black patch of skin in the centre of the area of erythema. The patient asks why her skin has turned black.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Haemosiderin deposition from leaked red cells
Thrombosis of small vessels with ischaemic necrosis

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain the black skin.
Black skin in necrotising fasciitis means **tissue necrosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The small vessels supplying the skin **thrombose**, so the skin becomes ischaemic and dies.

elim: Bilirubin makes skin yellow, not black.
Haemosiderin causes brown staining in chronic venous disease.
Toxins do not stimulate melanin; the colour is dead tissue.
Venous congestion makes skin dusky or purple but does not explain necrosis.

steps.x: **D. Thrombosis of small vessels with ischaemic necrosis.** Rule: black = dead.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man who injects drugs has a 24 hour history of severe pain in his right groin and thigh around an injection site. The skin shows mild erythema with an ill-defined edge, but he cries out when the area is lightly touched. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 90/54 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pain out of proportion to mild skin signs with septic shock in an injecting drug user is necrotising fasciitis. Cellulitis pain matches the redness and rarely causes shock.

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a painful, red thigh in a drug user.

clues: mild erythema with an ill-defined edge
cries out when the area is lightly touched
steps.x: Risk factor, poorly demarcated mild erythema, **disproportionate pain**, shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Necrotising fasciitis.**

elim: Cellulitis pain matches the signs and shock is unusual.
DVT gives a swollen limb without this degree of sepsis.
A pseudoaneurysm is a pulsatile mass, not spreading erythema.
Septic arthritis causes a hot, painful hip with restricted movement, not skin changes.

steps.x: **D. Necrotising fasciitis.** Pain out of proportion + sepsis + IVDU.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and dapagliflozin has a 2 day history of severe scrotal pain and fever. The scrotum and perineum are swollen and red with a poorly demarcated edge and a small black area. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 96/62 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum and perineum in a diabetic on an SGLT-2 inhibitor is Fournier's gangrene. The black area (necrosis) and sepsis rule out simple cellulitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a painful, red scrotum with sepsis.
Diabetes plus an **SGLT-2 inhibitor**, perineal spread, necrosis, sepsis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fournier's gangrene**: necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum.

elim: Epididymo-orchitis is a tender testis without skin necrosis or perineal spread.
Cellulitis does not cause black necrotic skin and shock.
A hernia gives a groin lump and bowel obstruction, not perineal skin necrosis.
Torsion is sudden testicular pain in a young male without fever or skin necrosis.

steps.x: **B. Fournier's gangrene.** Diabetic + gliflozin + scrotal necrosis.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman cut her forearm on broken glass 3 days ago. She now has rapidly spreading redness and swelling of the forearm with pain far worse than the appearance suggests. She is previously well. Blood cultures later grow beta-haemolytic, Gram-positive cocci in chains.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Type 2 necrotising fasciitis in a healthy person after a limb wound is most commonly Group A Streptococcus. Gram-positive cocci in chains, beta-haemolytic, confirms Streptococcus pyogenes.

steps.x: It asks for the organism.

clues: pain far worse than the appearance suggests
steps.x: Limb wound, disproportionate pain, healthy host: **type 2**. Chains = streptococci.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes).**

elim: C. perfringens is a Gram-positive rod causing gas gangrene.
E. coli is a Gram-negative rod, part of polymicrobial type 1 disease.
Pseudomonas is a Gram-negative rod.
S. epidermidis grows in clusters and is coagulase-negative, a line contaminant.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pyogenes.** Type 2 = Group A Strep.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has a red, hot, swollen left calf 1 day after an arthroscopy wound became infected. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg. The surgical team suspects necrotising fasciitis rather than cellulitis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination that supports their suspicion?
o: Calf tenderness with pitting oedema only
Fluctuant swelling with a central punctum
Pain out of proportion to the skin findings
practice.e: Pain out of proportion to examination findings is the hallmark of necrotising fasciitis and the feature that separates it from cellulitis.

steps.x: A finding question: which sign points to necrotising fasciitis over cellulitis?
Recent surgery and septic: they need the distinguishing sign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pain out of proportion** to what you can see.

elim: Calf tenderness and oedema suggest DVT.
A fluctuant swelling with a punctum is an abscess.
A sharply demarcated, raised edge is erysipelas; necrotising fasciitis is poorly demarcated.
Target lesions are erythema multiforme.

steps.x: **C. Pain out of proportion.** The hallmark.

practice.stem: A 59 year old woman with type 2 diabetes develops necrotising fasciitis of the vulva and perineum. Her medications are atorvastatin, dapagliflozin, gliclazide, metformin and ramipril. The microbiologist asks which drug is most likely to have increased her risk.
practice.q: Which is the most likely contributing cause?
practice.e: SGLT-2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin cause glycosuria, which promotes genital bacterial growth and is linked to Fournier's gangrene.

steps.x: A cause question: which drug raises the risk?
Genital necrotising fasciitis (Fournier's) and heavy **glycosuria**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **SGLT-2 inhibitor**: dapagliflozin.

elim: Statins cause myalgia, not genital infection.
Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain.
Metformin causes GI upset and rarely lactic acidosis.
ACE inhibitors cause cough and hyperkalaemia.

steps.x: **B. Dapagliflozin.** Gliflozin + genital necrotising fasciitis = Fournier's link.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man had a hip replacement 4 days ago. He now has severe pain around the wound, spreading purple discolouration with bullae and crepitus on palpation. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 84/50 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Severe pain, bullae, crepitus, septic shock and metabolic acidosis after surgery are late features of necrotising fasciitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a post-operative wound infection with shock.
Recent surgery, **late signs** (bullae, gas), shock, raised lactate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Necrotising fasciitis.**

elim: Cellulitis does not cause crepitus, bullae and shock.
Compartment syndrome causes pain on passive stretch without fever or crepitus.
Pyoderma gangrenosum is a sterile ulcer, not a septic illness with gas.
Thrombophlebitis is a tender cord along a vein.

steps.x: **C. Necrotising fasciitis.** Crepitus + bullae + shock after surgery.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has severe pain and mild erythema of the left thigh after a minor cut. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. A bedside ultrasound is performed while the surgeons are called.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on ultrasound?
o: Fluid and air between the fascial layers
practice.e: In necrotising fasciitis, ultrasound shows fluid and air between the fascial layers, indicating a deeper soft-tissue infection.

steps.x: A finding on ultrasound in suspected necrotising fasciitis.
Pain out of proportion after a minor injury: deep infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fluid and air along the deep fascia.**

elim: An isolated collection is an abscess.
A joint effusion suggests septic arthritis.
A non-compressible vein is DVT.
Oedema with normal fascia fits cellulitis.

steps.x: **B. Fluid and air between fascial layers.**

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with type 2 diabetes has necrotising fasciitis of the perineum. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. A venous blood gas is taken.
practice.q: Which is the most likely result on venous blood gas?
practice.e: Necrotising fasciitis with septic shock gives a metabolic acidosis from lactate due to poor tissue perfusion; the fast breathing is compensation.

steps.x: What will the gas show in a septic patient?
Shock means poor perfusion and **lactate**; the high RR blows off CO2 to compensate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metabolic acidosis with raised lactate.**

elim: Metabolic alkalosis follows vomiting or diuretics.
A shocked patient will not have a normal gas.
Respiratory acidosis needs hypoventilation; he is breathing fast.
Pure respiratory alkalosis ignores the lactate from shock.

steps.x: **A. Metabolic acidosis with raised lactate.**

practice.stem: A 50 year old man has suspected necrotising fasciitis of the right leg. IV fluids and antibiotics have been started. His pulse rate is 130 bpm and BP 82/48 mmHg despite 1 litre of fluid. A CT scan of the leg is booked for 2 hours' time.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Mark the erythema and review in 4 hours
Proceed to theatre for debridement now
practice.e: Imaging must never delay surgery. A shocked patient with suspected necrotising fasciitis needs emergency surgical debridement now.

steps.x: Next step in a deteriorating patient waiting for a scan.

clues: BP 82/48 mmHg despite 1 litre of fluid
steps.x: Refractory shock and a scan that delays surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Theatre now.**

elim: MRI delays surgery even more.
Watching the edge is for cellulitis; this is lethal delay.
A CRP will not change the decision.
Imaging must never delay surgery.

steps.x: **C. Proceed to theatre for debridement now.**

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has suspected necrotising fasciitis of the abdominal wall after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She has no drug allergies. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. The surgeons are preparing theatre.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?
practice.e: Empirical broad-spectrum IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin (or meropenem plus clindamycin) covers polymicrobial infection and clindamycin reduces toxin production.

steps.x: Which empirical antibiotics for necrotising fasciitis?
Septic, deep infection, possibly polymicrobial: **broad-spectrum IV** plus an anti-toxin agent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin.**

elim: Benzylpenicillin alone misses Gram-negatives and anaerobes.
Oral doxycycline is for mild infections.
Oral flucloxacillin is for cellulitis.
Trimethoprim is for urinary tract infection.

steps.x: **B. IV pip-taz plus clindamycin.**

practice.stem: A 68 year old man arrives with suspected Fournier's gangrene. The urology registrar is on the way to arrange theatre. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management while theatre is arranged?
o: Await a CT scan before giving antibiotics
IV fluid bolus, blood cultures and IV antibiotics
practice.e: The Sepsis Six (oxygen, cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate, urine output) is delivered immediately alongside arranging debridement.

steps.x: Immediate management before surgery.
Septic shock with lactate above 4: resuscitate now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sepsis Six**: fluids, cultures, IV antibiotics.

elim: Antibiotics must not wait for imaging.
Hyperbaric oxygen does not replace resuscitation or surgery.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate in septic shock.
Dressings do not treat a deep, spreading infection.

steps.x: **C. IV fluid bolus, blood cultures and IV antibiotics.**

practice.stem: A 36 year old man has necrotising fasciitis of the lower leg caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. At first the overlying skin looked only mildly red, yet at surgery there was extensive necrosis of the deep fascia.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism explaining the mild skin findings?
o: Deposition of immune complexes in the skin
Enzymatic spread along fascial planes beneath relatively spared skin
practice.e: Bacterial toxins and enzymes (hyaluronidase, streptokinase) spread along fascial planes with relative sparing of the overlying skin initially, so examination lags true severity.

steps.x: A mechanism: why does the skin look better than the fascia?

clues: extensive necrosis of the deep fascia
steps.x: The damage is **deep**, along the fascia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Toxins and enzymes spread **along fascial planes** while the skin is relatively spared.

elim: This is an infection, not a vasculitis.
Immune complex disease is not the mechanism.
IgE causes allergy, not necrosis.
Epidermal infection would make the skin look worse, not better.

steps.x: **C. Enzymatic spread along fascial planes.** The skin lags the fascia.
